title: Trump Stay-at-Home Parent Payment: How It Could Work and What You May Get
summary: A new draft rule could let married stay-at-home parents qualify for federal child care aid when their spouse works at least 35 hours per week.
body_markdown:
If you stay home with your children while your spouse works full time, a proposed Trump administration rule could make your family eligible for federal child-care assistance. The aid would come from the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), a federal-state program that helps lower- and middle-income working families pay for child care. The program provides approximately $9,000 in annual assistance per child, on average. The administration is seeking to make the change through federal rulemaking rather than legislation. The assistance is not yet available, as the rule is still being drafted.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=trumpstayathomeparentpayment) can help you plan for child care costs, savings and retirement based on your family’s income.**


## What the Draft Rule Would Change


According to The New York Times, the draft rule would allow married couples with one[stay-at-home parent](https://smartasset.com/taxes/stay-at-home-mom-with-kids-claiming-this-tax-credit-could-add-to-family-refund) to receive CCDF assistance. The other spouse would need to work at least 35 hours per week. The family must also meet the program’s income requirements.1


The money would be intended to help offset the income the stay-at-home parent gives up. The New York Times also reported that the plan is a top priority of Vice President JD Vance and could create the only federal subsidy that pays parents to stay home with their children.


The proposal involves the CCDF, a federal-state program with about $12 billion in annual federal funding. This amount includes roughly $8.75 billion in discretionary funding2 and $3.55 billion in mandatory and matching funds.3 The program was created in the 1990s and is administered by the Administration for Children and Families in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).


The current federal law allows parents who are working, in school or receiving job training to qualify, unless certain protective-services rules apply. Family income also generally cannot exceed 85% of the[state’s median income](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/heres-the-salary-it-takes-to-live-comfortably-in-each-u-s-state-in-2026) .4 According to The New York Times, states can set lower income limits, with some capping eligibility at 60% of the state median income.


Most CCDF money goes to states, which use it to help eligible families[pay for child care](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/cost-of-raising-a-child-in-major-u-s-metros-2026-study) through arrangements such as vouchers or payments to providers. The fund supports care for about 1.3 million children under age 13.5


The draft would create a new category known as “parent-based child care.” The administration is seeking to make the change through federal rulemaking rather than asking Congress to pass a new law.


According to The New York Times, the rule could still be revised before it’s published. The White House would need to approve it first, and the public would then have an opportunity to submit comments. If finalized, it could take effect as soon as 2027.


## Who Could Qualify


The draft wouldn’t pay every parent who stays home. Under the version reported by The New York Times, parents must be married, with[one spouse working](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/stayinghomeparent2026) at least 35 hours per week while the other cares for the child at home. The family also needs to meet CCDF income requirements for their state.


Some families could remain excluded. An[unmarried couple](https://smartasset.com/mortgage/how-to-buy-a-house-as-an-unmarried-couple) with one parent staying home would not qualify under the current draft. A[single parent](https://smartasset.com/retirement/college-vs-retirement-can-single-parents-save-for-both) who does not work is also ineligible.


For reference, the table below compares current program eligibility with the proposed change, as well as what households could expect under each:


### Current Child Care and Development Fund vs. Proposed Rule


Program Details Current CCDF Program Reported Draft Rule


Main purpose Help eligible families pay for child care while parents work, study or train Would also recognize care provided by a stay-at-home parent


Married couple, both working May qualify May qualify


Married couple, one working 35+ hours and one at home Generally not eligible on that basis Could qualify


Unmarried couple, one parent at home Generally not eligible on that basis Would not qualify


Single parent who does not work Generally not eligible Would not qualify


Income limit Generally up to 85% of state median income; states may set lower limits Existing income limits would still apply


## How Much Could Families Potentially Receive?


In fiscal year 2023, the Office of Child Care reported that CCDF payments to child care providers averaged $690 per child per month, or $8,280 annually.6 That figure comes from monthly state reports and excludes the copayments families pay. The average includes children of different ages and types of care, with payments for infant care averaging $929 per month.


To illustrate how much assistance families could receive, consider the following examples. Since federal data is already three years old, we use the more recent estimate from The New York Times, which reports that CCDF provides about $9,000 per child each year.


### How Much a Family Could Get Per Child


Children Illustrative Annual Assistance at $9,000 Per Child


1 $9,000


2 $18,000


3 $27,000


That does not mean every qualifying[stay-at-home parent](https://smartasset.com/taxes/trump-stay-at-home-mom-tax-credit) would automatically receive $9,000. States administer the program and have substantial control over eligibility, subsidy amounts and[how funds are distributed](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/federal-childcare-subsidies-2026) .


For another comparison, Child Care Aware of America estimated the national average annual price of child care at $13,184 in 2025.7 Using those figures for one child, $9,000 would equal roughly 68% of the national average annual price ($9,000 ÷ $13,184). Actual child-care prices vary significantly by state, age and type of provider.


## When Payments Could Start


This stay-at-home-parent benefit won’t be available until the rule is finalized. Federal agencies must follow a set process before a new rule can take effect, and some steps have no fixed timeline. The table below outlines each stage, based on guidance from the Office of the Federal Register:8


### How a Proposed Rule Takes Effect


Step What Happens Typical Timing


Draft proposal HHS writes the proposed rule No set timeline


White House review The White House’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs reviews significant rules before they’re published No set timeline


Proposed rule The rule is published in the Federal Register Starts the comment period


Public comment Individuals and organizations can submit feedback Generally 30 to 60 days, sometimes longer


Agency review HHS weighs the comments and can revise the rule or end the process No set timeline


Final White House review Significant final rules go back to the White House before publication No set timeline


Effective date The final rule takes effect after it’s published Generally at least 30 days later, or 60 days for a major rule


Many of these steps have no fixed deadline, so families should not build a household budget around receiving the money yet.


## Why Working Families Could See Less Funding


Critics warn that using existing CCDF funding to pay stay-at-home parents could reduce the money available to single working parents, unmarried couples and parents enrolled in school or job training.


The National Women’s Law Center, which opposes the proposal, says it would punish single mothers in particular. The group described the plan as part of an effort to “punish single mothers in the name of prioritizing ‘traditional families.'”9


The Office of Child Care, which runs CCDF, already said in its 2022 priorities report that the program only serves one out of every seven eligible children because of limited funds.10 A more recent federal estimate found that 1.8 million children received subsidies in 2022, which is 16% of the 11.8 million eligible under federal rules.11


Critics also say that redirecting part of the fund could reduce assistance for families who pay for outside care, putting more financial pressure on providers. Roughly 225,000 providers served children receiving CCDF help in fiscal year 2022.12


Supporters, on the other hand, welcome the change. They maintain that it would treat families more equally, whether they pay for outside care or have one parent provide it at home. They also argue that stay-at-home parents give up income to raise their children and, therefore, should have access to support too.


The idea behind the rule change appears in Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s policy blueprint for a Republican presidential administration, which was published ahead of the 2024 election.13 It calls for sending child care funding to parents to offset the cost of staying home, rather than to universal day care.


## **Bottom Line**


The proposed stay-at-home-parent payment would work through CCDF, the federal child care program that currently helps working families pay for day care. If HHS finalizes the rule as drafted, married couples who meet their state’s income limits could qualify when one spouse works at least 35 hours a week and the other stays home. Actual payments would depend on your state, and none are available until the rule takes effect.
